newsitem.title: USA: U.S. high court denies landlady's religious appeal.
newsitem.headline: U.S. high court denies landlady's religious appeal.

text.p: The Supreme Court on Friday rejected an appeal by a California landlady who refused to rent an apartment to an unmarried couple because of her religious beliefs.

The justices let stand a decision by the state supreme court that Evelyn Smith of Chico, California, violated state housing discrimination laws in 1987 by refusing to rent the one-bedroom unit to Gail Randall and Kenneth Phillips.

Smith, a Presbyterian, argued that renting to unmarried couples would violate her religious rights because she believes sex outside of marriage is a sin and that God would punish her by denying her eternal salvation.

The state charged that Smith, an elderly widow, had violated its 1980 fair housing law, which prohibits discrimination based on marital status, and the state Supreme Court ordered her to pay a $454 fine.

In appealing to the Supreme Court, Smith's attorneys argued that her actions were protected under the constitutional guarantee of religious freedom under the First Amendment and by the 1993 Religious Freedom Restoration law.
"This court should accept this case to determine whether California has a compelling state interest to justify its substantial burden on Mrs. Smith's rights," they said.

A number of religious groups representing Jews, Baptists and other denominations supported the appeal. The California Fair Employment and Housing Commission opposed the appeal, saying that Smith sought "the right to discriminate in business activities affecting the public interest."

Attorneys for the couple, who had been living together for more than five years, also argued against the appeal. They said Smith could hire a rental agent to insulate her from being offended by prospective tenants.
Although the Supreme Court this week struck down the 1993 law, it denied Smith's appeal without comment or dissent.
